vision.oneLine: How mutual funds are set up, classified, valued, charged and judged, and how every return and ratio is computed.
vision.why:
Mutual Funds is one of the most predictable AFM chapters: ICAI repeats the same sum types (NAV, returns, effective yield, plan yield, Sharpe, Treynor, tracking error, hedge fee, constant ratio plan) with new numbers, and now adds concept questions built from a single line of the study material.

The chapter is the bridge to Portfolio Management (Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen, formula plans) and to debt valuation (duration).

items: International vs offshore, FoF, CPOF, quant
Beta from Sharpe and Treynor, expected NAV
Hedge fund fee and the high-water mark

sixty: A mutual fund pools money into units; investors share in proportion to units held.
S-T-A-C: Sponsor 5 years and 40%; Trust two-thirds independent; AMC 50% independent; Custodian independent.
NAV = net assets ÷ units. A new investor does not change NAV; a dividend lowers it by the dividend per unit.
POP = NAV ÷ (1 − f). Redemption = NAV ÷ (1 + b). Required return = r₁ ÷ (1 − initial) + recurring.
Return = (change in NAV + distributions) ÷ opening NAV. Effective yield p.a. = period yield × 365 ÷ days.
Dividend reinvestment units = units × 10 × dividend % ÷ ex-dividend NAV. Bonus units = units × ratio.
Sharpe uses σ; Treynor uses β; Sortino uses downside σ. β = Sharpe × σ ÷ Treynor.
Beta moves only the equity part of NAV; cash falls by expenses.
Tracking error = standard deviation of (fund − benchmark), divided by n − 1.
Rates down: raise duration. Rates up: cut duration.
Constant ratio plan: fall buys, rise sells. Hedge fund incentive only above the high-water mark.

askedAs.how: NAV, loads, required return, returns, effective yield, plan yields, beta and expected NAV, tracking error, hedge fee, constant ratio plan, equalisation.
Compute Sharpe, Treynor and Jensen for several funds, rank them, comment.
Advantages, drawbacks, types of funds, role of manager, how to evaluate a fund.
Four options with a single computation or concept test.
SIP, side pocketing, quant funds, ETF vs index fund, international vs offshore.

pitfalls: Dividing recurring expenses by (1 − initial) in the required-return formula.
Using NAV instead of face value to get reinvestment units.
Applying beta to the whole NAV including cash.
Dividing tracking error by n instead of n − 1.
Charging the hedge fund incentive on the year's gain instead of the excess over the high-water mark.
Mixing front-end (÷ (1 − f)) and back-end (÷ (1 + b)) formulae.
Using 366 or the wrong day count in effective yield; ICAI counts from the entry date to the valuation date, excluding the first day.

levels.title: What a mutual fund is and how it is set up
levels.hook: Short-note marks: the four-part set-up and its numbers (5 years, 40%, two-thirds, 50%, 75%).

teach.html: A mutual fund is a trust that pools savings of many investors with a common goal, issues units, and invests in shares, debentures, bonds and money market instruments. Income and gains are shared in proportion to units held. The fund house charges a fee on the assets it manages. Think: Pool, Professionals, Proportionate share.

Sponsor: a body corporate in financial services for at least 5 years, financially sound; contributes at least 40% of the AMC's net worth. Trust: holds the property for unit holders; at least two-thirds of trustees are independent of the sponsor. AMC: SEBI-approved; net worth ₹100 crore per the SM; at least 50% independent directors; can be removed by a majority of trustees or by 75% of unit holders. Custodian: SEBI-registered, independent of sponsor and AMC, holds the securities.

teach.h: Why MFs help a small investor
teach.html: A well-diversified portfolio needs 15 to 20 stocks; with ₹5,000 that is impractical alone but possible through a fund. A SIP of ₹1,000 a month builds discipline. The SM also notes a fund does not pay capital gains tax when it sells a stock; an individual churning a portfolio does.

levels.correlate: The set-up numbers come back in the Law library, the match-up game and the "as written or twisted" game. The two-thirds (trustees) and 50% (AMC board) pair is the one students swap.

recall.q: Minimum years a sponsor must have been in financial services?
recall.why: 5 years.

recall.q: Sponsor's minimum contribution to the AMC's net worth (%)?
recall.why: At least 40%.

recall.q: Independent directors required on the AMC board?
recall.why: AMC board: at least 50%. Trustees: at least two-thirds.

recall.q: An AMC can be removed by 75% of the unit holders of the scheme.
recall.why: Or by a majority of the trustees.

recall.q: The custodian may be a group company of the AMC.
recall.why: The custodian must be independent of the sponsor and the AMC.

twist.q: A student writes "AMC: two-thirds independent directors; trustees: 50% independent". Spot the swap and give the correct pair.
twist.a: Swapped. Trustees: at least two-thirds independent of the sponsor. AMC board: at least 50% independent. Remember S-T-A-C in order: 5 years, 40% (sponsor); two-thirds (trust); 50% (AMC); independent (custodian).

levels.title: Classifying funds
levels.hook: Open, close, interval; equity and debt; ownership; direct and regular plans.

teach.html: Open-ended: enter and exit any time; capital unlimited. Close-ended: invest at the NFO or buy on the exchange; limited life; exit on the exchange, at expiry or in a repurchase period. Interval: open only at pre-specified intervals; need not be listed; no defined maturity. Capital Protection Oriented Funds, Real Estate MFs and FMPs are close-ended.
Equity: growth, aggressive, income. Debt: bond funds and gilt funds. Special funds: index, international, offshore, sector, money market, FoF, capital protection, gold, quant.
Public sector, private sector, foreign MFs. Direct plans (SEBI, 1 January 2013): no distribution expenses, trail fees or transaction charges, so NAV is generally higher than the regular plan.

levels.picture:
OpenCloseInterval
Buy / exitAny timeNFO, then exchangeAt set intervals
CapitalUnlimitedFixedFlexible at intervals
ListingNoYesNot required
levels.correlate: Close-ended funds trade away from NAV (Level 11, premium and discount). ETFs are close to NAV through the day (Level 3).

recall.q: Which must be close-ended?
recall.why: CPOFs, Real Estate MFs and FMPs are required to be close-ended.

recall.q: An interval fund must be listed on an exchange.
recall.why: Interval funds have an in-built redemption window and need not be listed.

recall.q: Direct plans were introduced by SEBI from…
recall.why: 1 January 2013.

recall.q: A direct plan generally has a lower NAV than the regular plan.
recall.why: No distribution costs, so NAV is generally higher.

recall.q: Liquidity of a close-ended fund comes mainly from…
opts: Repurchase by the fund any day
recall.why: Listing on the exchange (plus expiry or repurchase windows).

twist.q: A fund allows purchase and redemption only on the first working day of each quarter, is unlisted and has no maturity. Which type?
twist.a: Interval fund: open at pre-specified intervals at NAV-based prices, not required to be listed, no defined maturity.

levels.title: Special funds, schemes and ETFs
levels.hook: Concept questions: international vs offshore, capital protection, multicap, FMP, ETF.

teach.html: International: raises money in India, invests abroad. Offshore: located abroad, raises money globally to invest in India. Index: same weights as the index, passive, low cost. Capital Protection Oriented: protection is by portfolio structure, not a bank guarantee or insurance; close-ended, listed and rated. FoF: invests in units of other schemes. Quant: rule-based; models are tested on history and cannot be used blindly.

Multicap: at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps, rest at discretion. Flexicap: any proportion. ELSS: s.80C with a 3-year lock-in. FMP: close-ended debt fund whose investments mature with the fund, so no interest-rate risk but credit risk. Arbitrage: spot-futures differences. Dividend yield: medium risk.
ETF = index fund + share: listed, priced close to NAV, tradable all day through a broker. Authorised participants act as market makers. Types: index, commodity, bond, currency.

levels.correlate: FMP and interest-rate risk link to Level 4. Quant vs index manager links to tracking error in Level 10.

recall.q: A fund raises money in India and invests in foreign markets. It is…
recall.why: International = India to world. Offshore = world to India.

recall.q: Multicap: minimum % in each of large, mid and small caps?
recall.why: At least 25% each; the rest at discretion.

recall.q: A Capital Protection Oriented Fund is guaranteed by a bank.
recall.why: Protection comes from the portfolio structure, not from any guarantee or insurance.

recall.q: ELSS lock-in period in years?
recall.why: 3 years, s.80C.

recall.q: An FMP carries interest-rate risk but no credit risk.
recall.why: The reverse: its investments mature with the fund so interest-rate risk is avoided, but credit risk remains.

twist.q: A fund keeps 30% in large caps, 30% in mid caps, 10% in small caps. Can it call itself multicap?
twist.a: No. Multicap needs at least 25% in each of large, mid and small caps. 10% in small caps fails. It could be a flexicap, which has no minimum split.

levels.title: Debt funds: four risks and gilt duration
levels.hook: I-C-P-R, and the one rule for churning duration when rates are expected to move.

teach.html: Interest rate risk: bond value moves opposite to yields. Credit risk: issuer defaults. Prepayment risk: a callable bond is called early when rates fall. Reinvestment risk: proceeds reinvested at lower rates when rates fall; favourable when rates rise.

NAV = Σ(face value × price ÷ 100) ÷ units. To manage interest-rate risk the manager churns: rates expected to fall: raise duration (sell the shortest bond, buy the longest). Rates expected to rise: cut duration (sell the longest, buy a shorter one). Average duration (simple, as ICAI uses) = Σ durations ÷ n; revised = (Σ − sold + bought) ÷ n.

levels.picture: RTP Nov 2026 / MTP May 2026 example: average 7.85 years. Rates fall 25 bp: sell GOI 2026, buy GOI 2052, average becomes 9.75 years. Rates rise 75 bp: sell GOI 2052, buy GOI 2030, average becomes 6.55 years. ICAI does not buy the very short bond in the rising case.
levels.correlate: Duration is the bond-valuation idea of price sensitivity. Interest-rate risk is the same risk that an FMP avoids.

recall.q: An issuer calls a bond early because rates have fallen. This is…
recall.why: Callable bonds are called when rates fall: prepayment risk.

recall.q: If rates are expected to fall, the manager should lower average duration.
recall.why: Raise it: longer bonds gain more when rates fall.

recall.q: Order the steps to raise duration.
recall.why: Expect fall, sell shortest, buy longest, duration rises.

recall.q: Four bonds with durations 4, 6, 8, 10. Simple average duration?
Sell the 4-year bond and buy a 16-year bond (n stays 4). Revised average duration?

twist.q: Same fund, but rates are now expected to rise by 75 bp. A student sells the shortest bond. Why does ICAI not do that?
twist.a: To cut duration when rates rise you sell the longest bond and buy a shorter one. Selling the shortest raises duration, which is the wrong direction. ICAI also avoids buying a very short bond because a 75 bp move is large relative to its tiny maturity.

levels.title: NAV: what one unit is worth
levels.hook: The master formula of the chapter. Every other number hangs off NAV.

teach.html: NAV per unit = net assets ÷ units outstanding. Net assets = market value of investments + receivables + accrued income + other assets − accrued expenses − payables − other liabilities. NAV changes every day. Picture a pizza: net assets are the whole pizza, units are the slices; NAV is the value of one slice.

Listed shares at market price; shares bought at an index level can be scaled by the index: cost × present index ÷ base index; unlisted bonds at cost less diminution; cash at book; accrued income added.

teach.h: What changes NAV and what does not
teach.html: A new subscription issues units at the current NAV (cheque ÷ NAV) and leaves NAV unchanged on day one. After a dividend, NAV falls by the dividend per unit.

levels.correlate: NAV feeds loads (Level 6), returns (Level 7), plan yields (Level 8) and the evaluation sums (Level 10).

recall.q: Net assets ₹1,550 lakh and 155 lakh units. NAV (₹)?
A new investor's cheque changes the NAV on the day of issue.
recall.why: Units are issued at the current NAV, so NAV is unchanged on day one.

recall.q: Cum-dividend NAV ₹10, dividend ₹0.50 per unit. Ex-dividend NAV (₹)?
Shares bought at index 20,000 for ₹100 lakh; index now 22,000. Value (₹ lakh)?
Which item is deducted when computing net assets?
recall.why: Accrued expenses, payables and other liabilities are deducted.

twist.q: A fund has net assets ₹1,550 lakh and 155 lakh units. A new investor sends ₹31 lakh. What is the NAV afterwards?
twist.a: Units issued = 31 lakh ÷ 10 = 3.1 lakh. Net assets become 1,581 lakh and units 158.1 lakh. NAV = 1,581 ÷ 158.1 = ₹10, unchanged. Money in and units out at the same price cannot move the NAV.

levels.title: Loads, expenses and the return a fund must earn
levels.hook: Two divisions that trip everyone: POP = NAV ÷ (1 − f), redemption = NAV ÷ (1 + b).

teach.html: Entry (front-end) load is added to NAV at purchase; exit (back-end) load is deducted at redemption and goes to the scheme, not the AMC. ICAI formulae: POP = NAV ÷ (1 − f); Redemption price = NAV ÷ (1 + b). Alternative accepted: load = (POP − NAV) ÷ NAV; exit load = (NAV − redemption price) ÷ NAV. In dividend-equalisation sums ICAI simply uses NAV + load% × NAV and NAV − load% × NAV.

TER / MER: % of assets spent to run the fund; excludes brokerage on trading. SEBI maximum for equity funds 2.50%, excess borne by the AMC. Trail commission: 0.30% to 0.75% a year on daily average AUM, paid monthly; direct plans carry none.
r₂ = r₁ ÷ (1 − initial expenses) + recurring expenses. Gross up for initial, add on recurring. Example: r₁ 10%, initial 6%, recurring 2% gives 0.10 ÷ 0.94 + 0.02 = 12.64%.

levels.correlate: Loads change the price per unit, so they change units bought (Level 5) and the return you compute (Level 7). Direct plans save exactly the trail commission (Level 2).

recall.q: NAV ₹49, front-end load 2%. Public offer price (₹)?
NAV ₹50.50, back-end load 1%. Redemption price (₹)?
r₁ 12%, initial expenses 4%, recurring 1.5%. Required fund return (%)?
The exit load is income of the AMC.
recall.why: It goes into the scheme's pool.

recall.q: TER includes brokerage on portfolio trades.
recall.why: TER excludes brokerage.

twist.q: NAV ₹10, POP ₹10.204, redemption price ₹9.80. Find both loads. Two answers are acceptable for each: why?
twist.a: Front-end: by the ICAI formula f = 1 − 10 ÷ 10.204 = 2.0%; by the alternative (POP − NAV) ÷ NAV = 2.04%. Back-end: b = 10 ÷ 9.80 − 1 = 2.04%; alternative (NAV − RP) ÷ NAV = 2.0%. ICAI accepts both methods; state which one you use.

levels.title: Returns: holding period and effective yield
levels.hook: Change in NAV plus what was paid out, over what you paid. Then annualise.

teach.html: r = [(NAVₜ − NAVₜ₋₁) + I + G] ÷ NAVₜ₋₁ where I is income and G capital-gain distribution per unit. With reinvestment: extra units = distributions ÷ reinvestment NAV; return = (closing units × closing NAV − cost) ÷ cost. Reinvestment wins when the reinvestment NAV is below the closing NAV.

Yield p.a. = [(value gain) + dividends] ÷ investment × 365 ÷ days × 100. Units = investment ÷ entry NAV; value = units × closing NAV. Reverse: days = period yield × 365 ÷ yield p.a. Count days from the entry date to the valuation date, excluding the first day.
Monthly × 12 = annual (simple), as ICAI does. Back-solving NAV: annual 15% means monthly 1.25%, then solve for NAV.

levels.correlate: These are the building blocks of Level 8 (plan-wise yield) and the geometric return in Level 11.

recall.q: NAV 100 to 104, income ₹3 and capital gain ₹1 per unit. Return (%)?
Period yield 8% over 73 days. Yield p.a. (%)?
Period yield 8%, yield p.a. 40%. Days held?
Reinvesting distributions is better when the reinvestment NAV is above the closing NAV.
recall.why: Better when it is below: more units at a cheaper price.

recall.q: Annualised yield 24%. Yield for 5 months (%)?

twist.q: Investor puts ₹1,00,000 at NAV ₹20 (5,000 units). Fall to ₹18.50 in 30 days, no dividend. Yield p.a.?
twist.a: Loss = 5,000 × 1.50 = ₹7,500, i.e. −7.5% for the period. × 365 ÷ 30 = −91.25% p.a. The formula is the same; the sign carries through.

levels.title: Income options and plan-wise yield
levels.hook: Units tables for dividend reinvestment, bonus and growth: the longest SM sums.

teach.html: Growth: no intermittent income. Dividend payout: dividend paid, NAV falls. Dividend reinvestment: dividend buys units at the ex-dividend NAV. Bonus plan: free units in the ratio; a 1:5 bonus gives 1 for every 5.

Reinvestment units = units × face value (₹10) × dividend % ÷ ex-dividend NAV. Dividend % is on face value, not NAV. Bonus units = units × ratio. Growth: unchanged. Value = closing units × closing NAV, less STT and tax where the question says. Annual return = net gain ÷ investment × 12 ÷ months (IRR is the accepted alternative).
Short-term gain only on units acquired within the short-term period. ICAI note: under the 5th proviso to s.48, STT is not deductible in computing capital gains.

levels.correlate: Plan yields reuse effective yield (Level 7). The backwards versions (find units before a reinvestment or bonus) are RTP favourites.

recall.q: 1,000 units, 20% dividend on face value ₹10, ex-dividend NAV ₹25. Units from reinvestment?
1,000 units, 1:5 bonus. Bonus units?
Units after a 1:5 bonus are 1,200. Units before?
Dividend % is applied to NAV when computing reinvestment units.
recall.why: It is applied to face value (₹10).

recall.q: STT is deducted when computing capital gains (5th proviso to s.48).
recall.why: STT is not deductible.

twist.q: 1,000 units bought at ₹25 each. Plans end at: reinvestment ₹30 (units 1,080), bonus ₹25 (units 1,200), growth ₹31 (units 1,000). Which plan wins?
twist.a: Values: 1,080 × 30 = ₹32,400; 1,200 × 25 = ₹30,000; 1,000 × 31 = ₹31,000. Gains on ₹25,000: 29.6%, 20%, 24%. Reinvestment wins on these closing NAVs. Always build the units table first.

levels.title: Fund accounts and dividend equalisation
levels.hook: Cash build-up, closing NAV, and why a new investor pays for income already earned.

teach.html: Opening cash = funds raised − initial expenses − portfolio bought. Closing cash = opening + sales + dividends/interest − purchases − expenses paid − distributions. Closing net assets = closing cash + portfolio at market − arrears. Closing NAV = net assets ÷ units. Distribution = payout % × realised earnings, not unrealised appreciation.

A mid-period investor pays, and an outgoing investor receives, the undistributed income per unit accumulated so far, so that all unit holders get equal income. Issue price = NAV + entry load + income per unit; repurchase price = NAV − exit load + income per unit. Income per unit = undistributed income ÷ units outstanding.
An underwriter takes the unsubscribed units (commission 2%); chargeable management expenses are the lower of actual and the SEBI cap on average funds invested; uncollected dividend is a receivable.

levels.correlate: Equalisation is entry load (Level 6) plus income. The cash build-up is the NAV numerator (Level 5).

recall.q: Undistributed income ₹20 lakh, 100 lakh units. Income per unit (₹)?
NAV ₹20, entry load 2%, income per unit ₹0.20. Issue price (₹)?
NAV ₹20, exit load 1%, income per unit ₹0.20. Repurchase price (₹)?
Distribution is a percentage of unrealised appreciation too.
recall.why: It is a percentage of realised earnings: capital gains on sale plus dividends.

recall.q: Chargeable management expenses are the higher of actual and the cap.
recall.why: The lower of the two.

twist.q: Loads in an equalisation sum: opening NAV ₹20 is given. A student grows the NAV month by month before applying the load. Is that how ICAI does it?
twist.a: No. ICAI applies the load on the opening NAV given in the question and does not grow the NAV month by month. Read the question's base, not your own.

levels.title: Evaluating a fund: risk-adjusted ratios, beta and tracking error
levels.hook: The most ratio-heavy level. Learn what each ratio divides by, and which investor it suits.

teach.html: Every ratio is (Rₚ − R_f) ÷ risk. Sharpe divides by total risk σ (suits an undiversified investor). Treynor divides by beta (suits a well-diversified investor). Sortino divides by downside deviation. Jensen's alpha = Rₚ − [R_f + β(Rₘ − R_f)] (Beyond: it comes from the Portfolio Management chapter and appears in RTP/MTP ranking sums).

Excess return = Sharpe × σ. Then β = excess return ÷ Treynor = Sharpe × σ ÷ Treynor. Expected NAV after a market move: split NAV into equity and cash; equity changes by β × market change; cash falls by the period's expenses. Never apply beta to cash.
TE = √[Σ(d − d̄)² ÷ (n − 1)] where d = fund return − benchmark return. Dividing by n − 1, not n, is the usual trap. A passive manager wants TE near zero.
Portfolio, Person, Place: portfolio quality, the manager's track record, the fund house. Evaluate every 6 to 12 months; give an equity fund 3 to 5 years.

levels.correlate: Sharpe, Treynor and Jensen are shared with the Portfolio Management chapter. Tracking error connects to the information ratio (Level 12) and to the manager's role (Level 11).

recall.q: Which ratio uses beta in the denominator?
recall.why: Treynor = (Rp − Rf) ÷ β.

recall.q: Sharpe 2, σ 10, Treynor 16. Beta?
Sharpe suits a well-diversified investor.
recall.why: Sharpe uses total risk and suits an undiversified investor; Treynor suits a well-diversified one.

recall.q: Tracking error divides the sum of squared deviations by n.
recall.why: By n − 1.

recall.q: Differentials 3, 1, 1, −1, 1. Mean differential?

twist.q: NAV ₹80 with 95% in equity; Sharpe 2, σ 10, Treynor 16. Market falls 4%; monthly expenses ₹1. Expected NAV? Then redo for a +8% market.
twist.a: Equity 76, cash 4. β = 2 × 10 ÷ 16 = 1.25. Fall: equity × (1 − 5%) = 72.20; cash 4 − 1 = 3; NAV ₹75.20. Rise +8%: equity × (1 + 10%) = 83.60; plus 3 = ₹86.60. Beta only touches the equity part.

levels.title: Managers, FIIs, formula plans, hedge funds and closed-end funds
levels.hook: Four different numerical styles in one level: rebalancing, high-water mark, premium or discount.

teach.h: Role of the fund manager and FIIs
teach.html: Active managers aim for positive alpha; passive managers match the index with minimum tracking error. Four roles: C-M-W-O: Compliances, Monitoring, Wealth creation and protection, Outsourcing control. FIIs: Governance, Competition, Capital (G-C-C).

Keep a fixed ratio between equity and bonds; rebalance when NAV moves by the trigger (15% in the SM question, each month compared with the previous month). Total = bonds + units × NAV; reset each side to its share. Fall: buy. Rise: sell.
Fixed fee = % × assets. Incentive = % × (new value − high-water mark), only if positive. Trap: charging the incentive on the year's gain instead of the excess over the high-water mark.
Price = NAV × (1 + premium) or NAV × (1 − discount). The investor earns the price; the fund earns the NAV. Geometric return = (end ÷ start)^(1/n) − 1.
Stressed assets are separated so the main NAV reflects only liquid assets; avoids distress sales but has been misused.

levels.correlate: Formula plans are covered in detail in the Portfolio Management chapter. The hedge fund high-water mark echoes any performance-fee contract.

recall.q: In a constant ratio plan, when NAV falls the investor sells units.
recall.why: Fall: buy units to restore the ratio. Rise: sell.

recall.q: Hedge fund: assets ₹20 crore, return 29%, high-water mark ₹21 crore. Excess over the mark (₹ crore)?
Incentive 2% on that excess (₹ lakh)?
recall.why: 2% × 4.8 crore = 0.096 crore = ₹9.6 lakh.

recall.q: The investor in a closed-end fund earns on…
recall.why: The investor earns the price; the fund earns the NAV.

recall.q: Order the constant ratio rebalancing steps.
items: Set each side to its ratio share
recall.why: Trigger, total, target, trade.

twist.q: Same hedge fund, return only 4.5% with high-water mark ₹21 crore. Fee at 0.10% fixed and 2% incentive?
twist.a: New value = 20 × 1.045 = ₹20.90 crore, below the ₹21 crore mark, so no incentive. Fee is the fixed 0.10% × ₹20 crore = ₹2 lakh only.

levels.title: Beyond the study material: ideas that can be turned into questions
levels.hook: One line in the SM can become a full question. These concepts follow naturally from the chapter.

teach.h: SIP, STP, SWP and rupee-cost averaging (Beyond the SM)
teach.html: A SIP invests a fixed amount at intervals; a fixed amount buys more units when NAV is low. The average cost per unit is the harmonic mean of the NAVs, never above the simple average. It does not guarantee profit in a market that keeps falling. The SM mentions SIP only in passing.

teach.h: Jensen, M², information ratio, R² (Beyond the SM)
teach.html: Jensen's alpha: return above what CAPM requires for the fund's beta. M² = R_f + Sharpe × σ_market: the fund's return levered or de-levered to the market's risk. Information ratio = (Rₚ − R_b) ÷ tracking error. R² = correlation squared. Check any figure against the current source before using it.

NFO, AUM, AMFI, offer document, switch, folio, cut-off time. Exit load applies on switches too; ELSS restricts switch-out for the first 3 years. SEBI time limits and percentages change; check the circular before quoting a number.

levels.correlate: The tracking error of Level 10 plus the active return gives the information ratio. Expense ratio drag (formula bank) compounds over the years.

recall.q: SIP of ₹1,000 buys at NAV ₹10 then ₹20 (two instalments). Average cost per unit (₹)?
recall.why: Units 100 + 50 = 150 for ₹2,000: 2,000 ÷ 150 = 13.33, below the simple average 15.

recall.q: Rupee-cost averaging guarantees a profit.
recall.why: It lowers the risk of buying at a peak but does not guarantee profit in a falling market.

recall.q: Information ratio divides excess return over the benchmark by…
recall.why: Active return per unit of active risk.

recall.q: Exit load never applies on a switch between schemes.
recall.why: It applies on switches too (SM 6.2).

recall.q: The average cost per unit under a SIP equals…
opts: The arithmetic mean of the NAVs
The harmonic mean of the NAVs
recall.why: Total amount ÷ total units is the harmonic mean of NAVs.

twist.q: NAV is ₹10, ₹20 and ₹40 in three months and you invest ₹1,200 each month. Average cost per unit?
twist.a: Units = 120 + 60 + 30 = 210 for ₹3,600. Average cost = 3,600 ÷ 210 = ₹17.14, below the simple average of ₹23.33. The cheap month buys most units.

rows.b: Systematic (market) risk, beta against the fund's benchmark.

rows.a: An undiversified investor, for whom total risk matters.
rows.b: A well-diversified investor, for whom only market risk matters.

rows.a: Excess return over the risk-free rate.
rows.b: Excess return over the risk-free rate.

rows.a: Better: more return per unit of risk.
rows.b: Better: more return per unit of risk.

sorter.s: Divides excess return by standard deviation.

sorter.why: Total risk matters to an undiversified investor.

sorter.s: The numerator is return over the risk-free rate.
Given with σ to find excess return.
Given with excess return to find beta.

solves.title: NAV and new units
solves.tip: Keep everything in lakh. Add the assets in one go, then subtract the liabilities in one go. A NAV that comes out as a round number is usually right.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: A scheme (₹ lakh): shares at market 1,200; bonds 300; cash 50; receivables 20; accrued expenses 10; other payables 10. Units outstanding: 155 lakh.

variants.label: Twist 1: new investor
variants.q: Same scheme. A new investor sends a cheque of ₹31 lakh.

variants.label: Twist 2: dividend
variants.q: Same scheme. It now declares a dividend of ₹0.50 per unit.

variants.label: Twist 3: index scaling
variants.q: Of the 1,200 lakh of shares, ₹100 lakh worth was bought when the index was 20,000, and the index is now 22,000. The ₹100 lakh is currently carried at cost. Restate using the index.

steps.ask: Value of that block now (₹ lakh).
New net assets if the other 1,100 lakh of shares are at market (₹ lakh).
steps.say: Previously 1,550 with the block at 100; now 1,550 − 100 + 110 = 1,560.

solves.title: Loads: public offer price and redemption price
solves.tip: Pick the numbers so the division comes out clean: 49 ÷ 0.98 = 50 because 49 is 98% of 50. Front-end divides by (1 − f); back-end divides by (1 + b). Do not mix them.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: NAV ₹49 with a front-end load of 2%. Separately, NAV ₹50.50 with a back-end load of 1%. Use the ICAI formulae.

variants.label: Twist: find the loads
variants.q: NAV ₹10; public offer price ₹10.204; redemption price ₹9.80.

steps.ask: Front-end load by ICAI formula f = 1 − NAV ÷ POP (%).
steps.say: 1 − 10 ÷ 10.204 = 0.01999 = 2.0% (the alternative (POP − NAV) ÷ NAV gives 2.04%, also accepted).

steps.ask: Back-end load by ICAI formula b = NAV ÷ RP − 1 (%).

solves.title: Return a fund must earn
solves.tip: Two moves only: divide by (1 − initial) to gross up, then add recurring. For the reverse, subtract recurring first, then multiply by (1 − initial).

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: An investor can earn 12% on his own. The scheme has initial expenses of 4% and recurring expenses of 1.5% a year. What must the scheme earn?

variants.label: Twist: reverse
variants.q: The scheme earns a gross 14% with recurring expenses 2% and initial expenses 4%. What does the investor actually get?

solves.title: Holding period return and reinvestment
solves.tip: Numerator first: price change plus everything paid out. Divide by the opening NAV only. For reinvestment compare the two end values, not the two percentages in your head.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: Opening NAV ₹100, closing NAV ₹104. During the period the fund distributed income ₹3 and capital gains ₹1 per unit.

steps.ask: Total gain per unit: price change plus distributions (₹).

variants.label: Twist 1: reinvest
variants.q: Investor holds 1,000 units bought at ₹100 (cost ₹1,00,000). The ₹4 per unit distribution is reinvested at an average NAV of ₹102. Closing NAV ₹104.

variants.label: Twist 2: back-solve
variants.q: Annualised return 12%. Opening NAV ₹50. Distribution this month: income ₹0.30, capital gain ₹0.20 per unit. Find the closing NAV.

steps.say: Gain 0.50 is exactly the distributions (0.30 + 0.20), so the NAV change is nil: ₹50.

solves.title: Effective yield per annum
solves.tip: Work in whole units. Gain per unit × units, add dividends, divide by the investment: that is the period yield. Then multiply by 365 ÷ days. Choose days that divide 365 (73 × 5 = 365).

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: ₹1,00,000 invested at NAV ₹20. After 73 days the NAV is ₹21.20 and a dividend of ₹0.40 per unit was received.

variants.label: Twist 1: reverse
variants.q: Documents lost. The period yield was 8% and ICAI-style effective yield p.a. was 40%. How many days was the money invested?

variants.label: Twist 2: a loss
variants.q: ₹1,00,000 at NAV ₹20. After 30 days the NAV is ₹18.50, no dividend.

solves.title: Plan-wise units
solves.tip: Dividend percentage is on the face value of ₹10, never on NAV. Write the three plans as three one-line sums and compare the end values.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: 1,000 units bought at ₹25. A 20% dividend (face value ₹10) is declared at an ex-dividend NAV of ₹25. Plan A reinvests the dividend, Plan B gets a 1:5 bonus, Plan C is growth. Closing NAVs: A ₹30, B ₹25, C ₹31. Ignore tax.

steps.ask: Plan A units after reinvestment at ₹25.
Plan B units after a 1:5 bonus.
Which plan gave the highest return on ₹25,000?

variants.label: Twist: undo the bonus
variants.q: After a 1:5 bonus an investor holds 1,200 units. How many did he hold before?

variants.label: Twist: undo the reinvestment
variants.q: After reinvesting a 20% dividend (face ₹10) at ex-dividend NAV ₹25, an investor holds 1,080 units. How many before?

solves.title: Expected NAV from Sharpe, Treynor and beta
solves.tip: Order of operations: excess return, beta, equity move, cash less expenses, add. Beta touches only the equity part. With Sharpe 2 and σ 10, the excess return is 20 without a calculator.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: A fund has NAV ₹80 with 95% in equity and the rest in cash. Sharpe ratio 2, standard deviation 10, Treynor ratio 16. The market falls 4%. Monthly expenses are ₹1 and are paid from cash.

steps.ask: Equity and cash parts (equity value in ₹).
Expected NAV (₹): revised equity plus cash (4 − 1).

variants.label: Twist 1: market rises
variants.q: Same fund; the market rises 8% instead.

variants.label: Twist 2: different ratios
variants.q: Another fund: Sharpe 3, σ 5, Treynor 10. Find its beta.

solves.title: Tracking error
solves.tip: Choose to subtract the mean first: the deviations then add to zero (a free check). Remember n − 1.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: Fund returns over five quarters: 8, 5, 6, 3, 7 (%). Benchmark returns: 5, 4, 5, 4, 6 (%).

steps.ask: Mean differential d̄ where d = fund − benchmark (%).
Sum of squared deviations Σ(d − d̄)².

solves.title: Hedge fund fees
solves.tip: Compute the new value first, compare with the high-water mark, and only then take the percentage. If the new value is below the mark the incentive is zero.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: Assets ₹20 crore; fixed fee 0.10%; incentive 2% of value above the high-water mark of ₹21 crore. The fund returns 29%.

variants.label: Twist 1: below the mark
variants.q: Same fund; the return is only 4.5%.

steps.say: No incentive. Fixed fee only: ₹2 lakh.

variants.label: Twist 2: a fall
variants.q: Same fund; the return is −1.8%.

steps.say: The new value is below the mark; incentive nil. The fixed fee is on assets: ₹2 lakh (as in the SM answer).

solves.title: Constant ratio plan
solves.tip: Write total value, then half of it for each side. The units to trade are the gap in equity value divided by the NAV. Fall: buy. Rise: sell.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: ₹2,00,000 split 50:50 between bonds and units at NAV ₹50 (₹1,00,000 each, 2,000 units). Trigger: rebalance when NAV moves 15% or more from the last month. The NAV falls to ₹40.

variants.label: Twist: NAV rebounds
variants.q: After that rebalancing the plan holds 2,250 units and ₹90,000 of bonds. The NAV rises 20% to ₹48.

solves.title: Gilt duration churn
solves.tip: Rule first: rates down means duration up (sell shortest, buy longest); rates up means duration down. Then (sum − sold + bought) ÷ n.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: A gilt fund holds four bonds with durations 4, 6, 8 and 10 years. Rates are expected to fall; the manager sells the shortest and buys a 16-year bond.

variants.label: Twist: rates rise
variants.q: Instead rates are expected to rise. The manager sells the longest bond and buys a 3-year bond.

steps.say: Rates up means cut duration: sell the longest, buy a shorter one.

solves.title: Dividend equalisation prices
solves.tip: Income per unit first. Then both prices are the load-adjusted opening NAV plus that income. ICAI applies the load on the NAV given, no month-by-month growth.

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: Opening NAV ₹20. Undistributed income to date ₹20 lakh on 100 lakh units. Entry load 2%, exit load 1%.

solves.title: Closed-end premium and geometric return
solves.tip: Two returns, two bases: the fund earns the NAV; the investor earns the price. Square roots of familiar numbers: 1.21 → 1.1; 1.2705 is close to 1.127².

variants.label: Base case
variants.q: A closed-end fund's NAV grows from ₹20 to ₹24.20 over 2 periods. The investor bought at NAV (no premium or discount) and sells when the units trade at a 5% premium.

hooks.story: The scheme's net assets are the whole pizza; units are the slices. NAV is what one slice is worth. A new buyer pays for a slice at today's price, so the slice value does not change. A dividend takes a bite out of the pizza and hands it out, so every slice is worth less by that bite.

An entry load is a toll you pay when you drive in, so fewer rupees reach the road (fewer units). An exit load is a toll when you drive out. The toll booth of the exit load belongs to the scheme, not the AMC.

hooks.h: Sharpe and Treynor: runners on a hill
hooks.story: Both ask how much extra distance a runner covers for each unit of effort. Sharpe counts all the effort (total σ). Treynor counts only the effort caused by the hill itself (β). A runner who trains alone cares about all effort; one on a team that shares the effort cares about the hill.
The manager is paid a bonus only when the water rises above the highest tide line ever reached. If the sea drops and rises again to the old line, there is nothing new to pay for.

links.how: Same numerator, different risk: σ (total) versus β (systematic).
Excess return = Sharpe × σ; β = excess ÷ Treynor; beta then drives the expected NAV.
Issue price = NAV + load + income per unit to date.
Same gain over cost; yield p.a. scales it by 365 ÷ days.
Days = period yield × 365 ÷ yield p.a. Reverse the same formula.
Ex-dividend NAV = cum-dividend NAV − dividend per unit.
Reinvestment units are bought at the ex-dividend NAV.
Reinvestment buys units with the dividend at NAV; a bonus gives free units in a ratio and adjusts NAV down.
A direct plan saves exactly the trail commission and distribution costs.
The direction of money is reversed: India to world versus world to India.
FMP investments mature with the fund, so no interest-rate risk, but credit risk remains.
Sell the shortest bond and buy the longest.
The investor earns the market price; the fund earns the NAV. Premium or discount sits between them.
Higher recurring expenses push up the return the scheme must earn.
A passive manager aims for minimum tracking error; a quant or index fund is judged on it.
Under the 5th proviso to s.48, STT is not deductible when computing capital gains.
The same ratios are used there; Jensen's alpha comes from that chapter.
The SM says formula plans are covered in detail in the Portfolio Management chapter.
Duration measures price sensitivity to yields; the same idea applies to any bond.
ELSS is the equity scheme eligible for the s.80C deduction.
